To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the visual perception of optic flow, simulating forward motion over a flat horizontal plane, activates the dorsal cuneate cortex (area V3), the latero-posterio precuneate cortex, and the ventral surface of the occipito temporal lobe.
the visual motion of forward self-motion in a horizontal plane activates the dorsal visual stream in area V3, the ventral visual stream in the fusiform gyris, and the parietal lode in the precuneus.

there is no area in the brain specifically dedicated to the processing of motion, and that the processing of optical flow, a stimulus that simulates self-motion, involves the dorsal and ventral visual pathways, but does not involve area V5.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of visual perception.
the neural mechanisms of motion vision, with the aim of understanding the neural basis for the perception of motion and of spatial layout in the world.
the neural correlates of visual motion perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual system is not a modular structure, and the notion of a motion-specific area, such as V5, is an oversimplification.
the perception of forward motion is mediated by a network of areas in the dorsal and ventral pathways, with the parietal cortex playing an important role.
the visual perception of optic flow is mediated by a complex network involving areas V1/V2 and V3 in the dorsal stream and the fusiform gyris in the ventral stream.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a hierarchy of visual motion analysis, in which area V3 plays a key role in processing information about self-motion.

there is a hierarchy of motion analysis, with V3 as the first stage, and that the dorsal pathway is involved in processing the motion of the visual world, as opposed to the motion of objects in that world, which may be the province of the ventral pathway.
the dorsal and ventral streams of visual processing both contain areas that are specifically tuned to the analysis of motion in depth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
optical flow, which is a powerful stimulus for the perception of self-motion, does not activate area V5, and thus that V5 is not the sole locus of the perception of motion in depth.
the perception of motion in depth is a function of multiple areas in the visual cortex.
the perception of forward motion can be studied in humans using PET, and that it is not necessary to use complex stimuli to activate the motion processing pathways.
